Name: overthinking_feedback_circuit
Title: Breaking the Overthinking Loop: Identifying and Severing the Attention-Head Feedback Circuit that Drives Redundant Self-Verification
Short Hypothesis: Overthinking in reasoning models is sustained by a small, identifiable positive-feedback circuit: a few attention heads write an 'uncertainty/keep-checking' direction into the residual stream that later reflection tokens (e.g., 'wait', 'but', 'let me verify') read from, which in turn re-triggers those heads. Severing this specific head-to-reflection-token read path—rather than uniformly steering hidden states—breaks the loop and shortens reasoning with minimal accuracy loss, and does so more surgically and interpretably than difference-vector steering.
Related Work: Recent training-free efficient-reasoning methods steer whole hidden states with difference vectors (SEAL, CATS, PID-steering) or rebalance reflection-marker logits at uncertain states (PathCal, ACTS). RISE uses SAEs to find and amplify/suppress reasoning-behavior directions. All treat redundancy as a hidden-state property or coarse marker-level signal; none isolate a *causal feedback circuit* at the attention-head level that mechanistically explains why models keep re-entering verification loops. Our proposal is distinct: we localize the specific heads that produce a self-reinforcing 'uncertainty broadcast' consumed by reflection tokens, verify the loop causally with path patching, and intervene by cutting the head->reflection-token read path (attention-pattern edit at specific query positions) rather than adding a global steering vector. This yields both a novel mechanistic account of overthinking and a more targeted, interpretable efficiency intervention.
Abstract: Reasoning models frequently overthink, spending many tokens re-verifying answers via reflection cues like 'wait', 'but', and 'let me check.' We hypothesize that this behavior is not diffuse but is driven by a compact positive-feedback circuit: a small set of attention heads write an 'uncertainty' direction into the residual stream that is preferentially read at reflection-token query positions, whose generation re-activates those heads, sustaining the loop. We test this by (1) locating heads whose output projections align with an uncertainty direction derived from contrasting long-verifying vs. concise traces, (2) measuring, at reflection-token positions, how much the query attends to and reads from these heads' outputs, and (3) using path patching to causally confirm that this head->reflection-token read path controls whether the model continues verifying or exits. We then introduce a training-free intervention that attenuates this specific read path—by masking or down-weighting the identified heads' contribution only at reflection-token query positions—breaking the feedback loop while leaving normal computation intact. We evaluate accuracy-vs-tokens Pareto curves on GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA across DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen2.5-7B, comparing against SEAL/CATS-style global steering and PathCal-style logit rebalancing. We expect 25-40% token reduction at equal accuracy with a more surgical, interpretable intervention, plus a mechanistic explanation of overthinking as a localizable circuit-level phenomenon rather than a global representational bias.
Experiments: 1. Uncertainty direction & head localization: Collect matched long-verifying vs. concise CoT traces (via prompting/temperature or self-consistency splits) on GSM8K/MATH/ProntoQA. Compute a residual-stream 'uncertainty' direction (difference-of-means at reflection-token positions). For each attention head, measure cosine alignment of its output-to-residual projection with this direction; rank candidate 'loop-driver' heads. 2. Feedback measurement: At reflection-token query positions, quantify (a) attention mass onto positions where loop-driver heads previously wrote, and (b) via the value-weighted read, how much the reflection token's next-token distribution shifts toward continued verification. Correlate head activity with subsequent reflection-token emission to establish the loop. 3. Causal validation with path patching: Patch the loop-driver-head outputs (from a concise-trace run into a long-trace run) specifically along the path to reflection-token query positions; measure whether the model exits verification earlier (reduction in subsequent reflection markers and total tokens) without answer change. Compare to random-head and random-position patching controls. 4. Intervention: Training-free decoding-time method that, at reflection-token query positions (detected online via top-k marker tokens), zeroes or down-weights the loop-driver heads' contribution (attention-pattern edit / head-output scaling). Sweep intervention strength. 5. Evaluation: accuracy vs mean tokens (Pareto), wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, SEAL/CATS-style global difference-vector steering, PathCal-style marker-logit rebalancing, and fixed truncation. Metrics: accuracy, tokens generated, number of reflection markers, fraction of preserved answers. 6. Ablations: number of heads intervened, layer distribution of loop-driver heads, restricting intervention to reflection positions vs. all positions, cross-dataset and cross-model transfer of identified heads, and whether the same heads generalize to non-math logic tasks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Overthinking may be mediated by many distributed heads rather than a compact set, weakening the 'circuit' story; head-ranking and path-patching controls quantify how localized it is. 2. Some verification loops are beneficial for hard problems; aggressive severing could hurt accuracy—the Pareto and per-difficulty analysis address this. 3. Online detection of reflection-token query positions is imperfect; we test robustness to the marker set. 4. Identified heads may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring per-model localization (cheap, done once). 5. Difference-of-means uncertainty direction may conflate multiple factors; SAE-based or probe-based alternatives serve as robustness checks.
